paragraphs.text:
By the same Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa: On the Medium. A Letter to Bishop Theodosius

He who said to his disciples, "Seek, and you will find," will surely also give the power to find to those who, out of love of learning, search as the Lord commanded and seek out the hidden mysteries. For he who made the promise does not lie, and in the generosity of his gifts he lavishes on us more than we ask. "Therefore attend to reading, my child Timothy." It is fitting, I think, to use the words of the great Apostle in addressing your goodness: "and may the Lord give you understanding in all things," so that you may be "enriched in every word and in all knowledge." As for the matters you instructed me to deal with, I have judged it right to serve your eagerness briefly, with whatever the Lord may suggest to me. In this way you may learn that we ought to serve one another in love by doing what the other wishes. First, then, since the question about the meaning of the passage on Samuel was placed before the other headings, I shall explain it as briefly as I can, God granting. Some of those before us have chosen to think that the sorceress really did conjure up Samuel. They offer an argument of this kind in support of their opinion. Samuel was grieved at Saul's rejection, and he kept pleading before the Lord [?] that Saul had purged from the people the sorcery practised by mediums to deceive people. The prophet was therefore distressed that the Lord would not be reconciled to the rejected man. And so, they say, God allowed the prophet's soul to be brought up through this kind of trickery, so that Samuel might know that he had put forward falsehoods to God on Saul's behalf when he said that Saul was hostile

to the mediums, since at that very moment Saul was using their sorcery to obtain the ascent of Samuel's soul. But I look to the gulf spoken of in the Gospel. The patriarch, or rather the patriarch's Lord, says that it has been fixed between the evil and the good, so that the condemned cannot go up to the rest of the righteous, and the saints cannot cross over to the company of the wicked. For this reason I do not accept such opinions as true, since I have been taught to believe that the Gospel alone is true. Samuel is great among the saints, and sorcery is a wicked possession. So I am not persuaded that Samuel, once established in so great a rest of his own, crossed that impassable gulf toward the ungodly, whether willingly or unwillingly. He could not have suffered it against his will, because the demon could not cross the gulf, enter the company of the holy, and move the saint from his place. Nor would he have done it willingly, because he neither wished nor was able to mingle with the wicked. For one who dwells among good things has no wish to move from where he is to the opposite. And even if one were to grant that he wished it, the nature of the gulf does not allow anyone to pass. What, then, is our view of these matters? The common foe of all is the enemy of human nature. His every scheme and effort is aimed at striking man in his most vital part. And what blow against human beings could be more deadly than to be cast away from God, who gives life, and to desert of one's own accord to the ruin of death? Those who love the body are eager, all through life, to have some knowledge of the future, by which they hope either to escape evils or to be guided to what they desire. For this reason the deceitful nature of the demons has devised many ways of knowing the future, so that people may not look to God. Among them are augury, the reading of omens, oracles, divination from livers, necromancy, ecstatic frenzies, possessions, inspirations, and many other such things. And whatever kind of foreknowledge someone has been deceived into believing true, that deceiving demon shows itself alongside it to confirm the deluded opinion of the one led astray. So the demon arranges for the flight of the eagle to agree with the observer's hope. It does the same with the quivering of the liver, the derangement of the brain's membranes caused by vapours, and the rolling of the eyes. The demon's cunning displays to its dupes each sign just as the deception has taught them to watch for it. In this way people depart from God and devote themselves to the service of the demons, through whom they believe such things are brought about. One form of this deception was the practice of the mediums, whose trickery was believed able to draw the souls of the departed back up to the life above. Saul had despaired of being saved, because the whole foreign nation had mustered its entire army against him. So he hit on the idea of having Samuel propose some way of safety to him. Then the demon that attended

the medium, by which the woman had habitually been deceived, took on various shadowy forms before her eyes. Saul could see none of the things the woman beheld. As soon as she began her sorcery and the phantoms were before her eyes, the demon devised a proof that what appeared was real. First it revealed who the man hidden under the disguise was. This astonished Saul all the more, as though the woman could no longer be mistaken about anything, since the commoner's clothing had not hidden the truth from her magic power. Now she said that she had seen gods coming up, and a man standing upright, wrapped in a double cloak. How, then, will the slaves of the letter maintain the literal sense? If it was truly Samuel who was seen, then the gods seen by the sorceress were truly gods as well. But Scripture calls the demons gods: "For all the gods of the nations are demons." Was the soul of Samuel, then, among the demons? Far from it! Rather, the demon that always obeyed the sorceress brought other spirits along with it, to deceive both the woman herself and Saul, who was being deceived through her. It made the medium take the demons for gods, while it took the form of the one being sought and imitated his voice. Then it uttered, in the guise of a prophecy, what could reasonably be inferred from appearances, the outcome that might be expected to follow in the natural course of things. But the demon also gave itself away against its will by speaking the truth: "Tomorrow you and Jonathan will be with me." For if it really was Samuel, how could a man condemned for every kind of wickedness come to be with him? Clearly it was that wicked demon, appearing in Samuel's place, which told no lie when it said that Saul would be with it. And if Scripture says, "And Samuel said," such a phrase should not trouble the discerning reader. Let him understand that the words "the one thought to be Samuel" are implied. For we find that Scripture often makes a habit of describing what seems to be in place of what is. Take the case of Balaam. At one point he says, "I will hear what God will say in me." Later we read, "When Balaam saw that it pleased God that he should not curse the Israelites, he no longer went as usual to meet the omens." The careless reader will suppose that there too it was the true God who spoke with Balaam. But what follows shows that Scripture used this name for the god Balaam believed in, and not for the God who truly is. So here too the one who seemed to be Samuel imitated the words of the true Samuel, and the demon cleverly mimicked prophecy from what was probable. The case of Elijah needs fuller study, but it does not belong to the question before us. When he was commanded to drink water from the brook, God was secretly guiding him to undo the sentence of drought that the prophet himself had pronounced against the Israelites. For he was permitted to drink only from the brook, and the brook would naturally

dry up in the drought. Since he was forbidden to drink from anywhere else, the prophet could find no other relief for his thirst, and so he was compelled to ask for rain, so that the brook would not run out of water. Meanwhile, the ravens served the prophet with what he needed to live. Through this God showed the prophet that many people had remained faithful to the worship of the true God, and that it was from them that the ravens brought him his food. For the ravens would not have brought him defiled bread or meat sacrificed to idols. So this too was meant to lead Elijah to relax his anger against the ungodly somewhat, as events taught him that many people look to God, and that it is not just to condemn them along with the guilty. The bread was given to him in the morning and the meat in the evening. Perhaps what happened holds, in the form of a riddle, an encouragement to the virtuous life: that beginners must [?] the more perfect things. As Paul puts it, "Solid food is for the mature, whose faculties have been trained by practice." As for the veil of Moses, you will know what it refers to once you have studied Paul's Epistle to the Corinthians. On your questions about the sacrifices, you would do well to examine the whole of Leviticus more carefully and, with more sustained attention, to consider the law in these matters as a whole. In this way the part will be understood together with the whole, since this part could not be made clear on its own before the whole has been studied. As for the difficulties you raised about the opposing power, the solution is plain. The one who became the apostate was not simply an angel, but held a rank among the archangels. It is clear, then, that his rule implies the order of beings under his command. This settles the question of how he was one and yet is now with a multitude: the host under his command rebelled together with him, and so the question is answered. The last heading you asked about is how the Spirit comes before baptism. This needs a broader examination and study, so we shall treat it in a separate work and, God granting, send it to your reverence.
